blocks.text: Velocity-time-graph helps you visually understand how the velocity of an object changes with time. It is used to:

items: Study motion in different time intervals clearly and effectively

blocks.text: In a velocity-time graph, the velocity (\(v\)) is plotted on the \(y\)-axis, and time (\(t\)) is plotted on the \(x\)-axis.

blocks.title: Teaching note

blocks.text: Key Features of Velocity-Time Graph
1. Slope of the graph \(\left(\frac{dv}{dt}\right)\), represents acceleration of the particle.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why the slope? For a straight segment the slope is \(\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\), the change in velocity divided by the time taken. That is exactly the definition of acceleration from 7.1.3. For a curve, the slope of the tangent at a point is \(\frac{dv}{dt}\), the instantaneous acceleration. Units follow the axes: (m/s) per s \(=\) m/s\(^2\).
• If a particle is moving with constant acceleration, its velocity-time graph is a straight line.

items: If \(a = \frac{dv}{dt} = 0\), the velocity-time graph is a horizontal straight line. In Figure 7.4, the particle is moving with uniform velocity from point \(B\) to point \(C\).

If \(a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \text{constant} > 0\), the velocity of the particle is increasing with increase in time, and the velocity-time graph is a rising straight line. In Figure 7.4, the particle is moving with positive uniform acceleration from point \(A\) to point \(B\).

If \(a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \text{constant} < 0\), the velocity of the particle decreases with increase in time, and the velocity-time graph is a falling straight line. In Figure 7.4, the particle is moving with uniform negative acceleration (retardation) from point \(C\) to point \(D\).

blocks.alt: Velocity-time graph with v on the vertical axis and t on the horizontal axis. A straight line rises from A to B (labelled a > 0), stays horizontal from B to C (labelled a = 0), then falls from C to D (labelled a < 0).
blocks.caption: Figure 7.4: velocity-time graph with uniform acceleration (A to B), uniform velocity (B to C) and uniform retardation (C to D) (original drawing after the textbook's figure; axis and BC labels corrected)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Figure 7.4 is a velocity-time graph, but the book labels its vertical axis \(x\) and writes "\(v = 0\)" on the segment BC (both copied from Figure 7.1, the displacement-time graph). Correct: the vertical axis is \(v\), and on BC the velocity is constant (not zero), so the label should be \(a = 0\). The text itself says the particle moves with uniform velocity from \(B\) to \(C\). Our drawing uses the corrected labels.

blocks.title: Recall!
blocks.text:
• Displacement = Area under velocity-time graph
• Acceleration = Slope of velocity time graph
• If a particle is moving with variable acceleration, then its velocity-time graph is not a straight line. (See Figure 7.5)

blocks.alt: Velocity-time graph drawn as a smooth curve that rises to a peak and then falls, showing variable acceleration.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.5: a curved velocity-time graph, variable acceleration (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: A straight line has the same slope everywhere, so a straight velocity-time graph means the same acceleration at every instant. In Figure 7.5 the curve gets less steep, becomes flat at the top (acceleration zero there for a moment) and then slopes downwards (negative acceleration). The acceleration keeps changing, so the graph bends. For such motion the equations of 7.1.6 cannot be used; we use calculus instead.

2. If \(A\) is the area under the velocity-time graph and above the time-axis from \(t = t_{1}\) to \(t = t_{2}\), then from integral calculus:
\[A = \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} v(t)\,dt\]
Since \(v = \frac{dx}{dt}\), we have:
\[A = \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} \dfrac{dx}{dt}\,dt\]
\[= \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} dx\]
\[= x(t_{2}) - x(t_{1})\]
Thus, \(A\) = displacement of the particle during the time interval from \(t_{1}\) to \(t_{2}\).

blocks.title: Recall!
blocks.text: If \(y = f(x) \ge 0\) for \(a \le x \le b\), then the area under the curve \(y = f(x)\), above the \(x\)-axis, and between the vertical lines \(x = a\), \(x = b\) is equal to \(\int_{a}^{b} y\,dx\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Start from the simplest case. If a car moves at a constant 20 m/s for 5 s, its graph is a horizontal line at height 20, and the region under it is a rectangle of area \(20 \times 5 = 100\). The car also covers \(20 \times 5 = 100\) m. So "velocity \(\times\) time" is the area. When the velocity changes, we cut the time into very thin strips; in each strip the velocity is almost constant, so each strip's area is (almost) the small distance covered. Adding all strips is exactly what the integral \(\int v\,dt\) does. The last step uses the Fundamental Theorem: \(\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} \frac{dx}{dt}\,dt = x(t_{2}) - x(t_{1})\), the change in position.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text:
If velocity-time graph lies both above and below the time axis, and \(A_{1}\) is area above time axis and graph, while \(A_{2}\) is the area below time axis and graph, then:
\[\text{Displacement} = A_{1} - A_{2}\]
\[\text{Distance} = A_{1} + A_{2}\]

blocks.alt: Velocity-time curve shaped like a wave that crosses the t-axis. Between two vertical lines, the region above the t-axis and under the curve is shaded and labelled A1; the region below the t-axis and above the curve is shaded and labelled A2.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.6: area A1 above the time axis and area A2 below it (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Below the time axis the velocity is negative: the particle is moving backwards. Distance moved backwards cancels part of the forward distance in the displacement, so we subtract \(A_{2}\). Distance counts every metre travelled, forwards or backwards, so we add. Remember that \(A_{1}\) and \(A_{2}\) are both taken as positive numbers here. (The integral \(\int v\,dt\) over the whole interval gives \(A_{1} - A_{2}\) automatically, because the part below the axis comes out negative.)

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: In graph questions: read the axis units first (minutes or hours, m/min or km/h); split the region under the graph into rectangles, triangles and trapeziums; use slope for acceleration and area for displacement. Never mix units: m/min \(\times\) min gives m.

blocks.alt: Velocity-time graph with v from 0 to 6 and t from 0 to 12. Horizontal line from A(0, 6) to B(8, 6), then a straight line down to C(12, 0). A dashed vertical line joins B to D(8, 0). O is the origin.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.7: velocity-time graph of the cyclist in Example 5 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Example 5
blocks.problem:
Figure 7.7 is the velocity-time graph for a cyclist traveling in a straight line. (The time is in minutes and velocity is in meters per minute).
(a) Calculate the total displacement of the cyclist from his starting position at the end of the 12 minutes.
(b) Determine the uniform deceleration during the final 4 minutes of motion.
steps:
Given: the velocity-time graph in Figure 7.7. The velocity is 6 m/min from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 8\) min (segment AB), then falls uniformly to 0 at \(t = 12\) min (segment BC).
To find: (a) the total displacement in 12 minutes; (b) the uniform deceleration during the last 4 minutes.
Method: displacement = area under the velocity-time graph; acceleration = slope of the graph. The region under the graph is the trapezium OABC.

Solution (a): set up the area
Let \(x\) be the total displacement. The displacement is equal to the area under the velocity-time graph, which is the area of trapezium OABC:
\[x = \text{Area of trapezium } OABC\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}(a + b)h \quad \text{...(1)}\]
Why: AB and OC are both horizontal, so they are the pair of parallel sides; OA is perpendicular to both, so it is the height. (See the Area of Trapezium box below.)

Identify \(a\), \(b\), \(h\)
\(a\) = length of lower side \(\overline{OC} = 12\),
\(b\) = length of upper side \(\overline{AB} = 8\), and
\(h\) = vertical distance between \(\overline{OC}\) and \(\overline{AB} = 6\).
Why: O is at \(t = 0\) and C at \(t = 12\); A is at \(t = 0\) and B at \(t = 8\); the height is the velocity 6 m/min.

Substitute into equation (1)
\[x = \dfrac{1}{2}(12 + 8) \times 6\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 6\]
\[= 60 \text{ meters}\]
Why: the units are (m/min) \(\times\) (min) \(=\) m.

Solution (b): slope of BC
Let \(a\) be the acceleration during the final 4 minutes of motion, then:
\[a = \text{slope of } \overline{BC}\]
\[= \dfrac{0 - 6}{12 - 8}\]
\[= -\dfrac{6}{4} = -\dfrac{3}{2} \text{ m/min}^{2}\]
Why: slope \(= \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\) from B(8, 6) to C(12, 0) is the acceleration. The minus sign means the velocity is decreasing: a deceleration of \(\frac{3}{2}\) m/min\(^2\).

Check:
Split OABC into rectangle OABD and triangle BDC:
\[8 \times 6 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 6 = 48 + 12 = 60\]
And with \(a = -\frac{3}{2}\) for 4 minutes the velocity falls by \(\frac{3}{2} \times 4 = 6\), from 6 to 0, as the graph shows.
blocks.answer: (a) Total displacement \(x = 60\) m. (b) \(a = -\frac{3}{2}\) m/min\(^2\), i.e. a uniform deceleration of \(\frac{3}{2} = 1.5\) m/min\(^2\).

blocks.title: Area of Trapezium
blocks.text:
A trapezium (trapezoid) is a four-sided plane figure that has exactly one pair of parallel sides. If \(a\) and \(b\) are the lengths of parallel sides and \(h\) is the perpendicular distance between them, then the area is given by:
\[\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}(a + b) \times h\]

blocks.alt: Velocity-time sketch. The line starts at A(0, u) on the v-axis, rises to B(3, 70), stays level to C(6, 70), then drops to D(6.5, 0) on the t-axis. Dotted lines: from B down to E(3, 0), from A across to F(3, u), from the 70 mark across to B, and from C down to t = 6. O is the origin.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.8: velocity-time sketch of Ali's drive in Example 6 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Example 6
blocks.problem:
Ali drives a car 400 km in a straight line. Figure 7.8 is a sketch of a velocity-time graph representing his motion. Ali starts with a velocity of \(u\) km/h and accelerates to a velocity of 70 km/h in 3 hours. He then maintains his velocity for 3 hours, after which he slows down uniformly to rest over the next \(\frac{1}{2}\) hour. Find:
(a) The value of \(u\)
(b) The acceleration of Ali during the first 3 hours of his drive.
steps:
Given: total displacement 400 km; velocity rises uniformly from \(u\) to 70 km/h in the first 3 h (A to B), stays 70 km/h from \(t = 3\) to \(t = 6\) h (B to C), then falls uniformly to 0 in the next half hour, at \(t = 6.5\) h (C to D).
To find: (a) \(u\); (b) the acceleration in the first 3 hours.
Method: the area under the graph equals the displacement (400 km); this gives one equation in \(u\). The acceleration is the slope of AB.

Solution (a): split the area
Since the displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph:
\[x = \text{area of } OABE + \text{area of } BCDE\]
\[x = \tfrac{1}{2}(a + b) h_{1} + \tfrac{1}{2}(c + d) h_{2}\ \text{...(1)}\]
Why: the dotted line BE (at \(t = 3\)) cuts the region into two trapeziums. OABE has vertical parallel sides OA and BE; BCDE has horizontal parallel sides BC and ED.

Identify the lengths
\(a = |OA| = u\), \(b = |BE| = 70\), \(h_{1} = |OE| = 3\)
\(c = |BC| = 6 - 3 = 3\), \(d = |ED| = 6.5 - 3 = 3.5\), \(h_{2} = b = 70\)
Why: in OABE the parallel sides are vertical, so the height is the horizontal width \(OE = 3\). In BCDE the parallel sides are horizontal, so the height is the vertical distance 70.

Substitute these values into equation (1)
\[x = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + 70)\times 3 + \tfrac{1}{2}(3 + 3.5)\times 70\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}(3u + 210 + 455)\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}(3u + 665)\]
Why: \((u + 70) \times 3 = 3u + 210\) and \(6.5 \times 70 = 455\); the common factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) is taken out.

Use \(x = 400\)
\[400 = \dfrac{1}{2}(3u + 665)\]
\[800 = 3u + 665\]
\[3u = 135\]
\[u = \dfrac{135}{3} = 45 \text{ km/h}\]
Why: multiply both sides by 2 (the step the book leaves out), then subtract 665 and divide by 3.

Solution (b): slope of AB
Let \(a\) be the acceleration during the first 3 hours of his drive:
\[a = \text{slope of } \overline{AB} = \dfrac{|BF|}{|AF|} \quad \text{...(1)}\]
where \(|BF| = |BE| - |EF| = 70 - u = 70 - 45 = 25\) and \(|AF| = |OE| = 3\).
Why: F is level with A, so BF is the rise in velocity (from \(u\) to 70) and AF is the time taken (3 h). (The book numbers this equation (1) again.)

Substitute
\[a = \dfrac{25}{3} \approx 8.33 \text{ km/h}^{2}\]
Why: acceleration has units (km/h) per hour \(=\) km/h\(^2\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. In a velocity-time graph, \(v\) is on the vertical axis and \(t\) on the horizontal axis.
2. Slope \(\frac{dv}{dt}\) = acceleration: horizontal line \(a = 0\), rising line \(a > 0\), falling line \(a < 0\) (retardation), curve = variable acceleration.
3. Area under the graph from \(t_{1}\) to \(t_{2}\) = \(\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} v\,dt\) = displacement.
4. Graph above and below the axis: displacement \(= A_{1} - A_{2}\), distance \(= A_{1} + A_{2}\).
5. Break the region into rectangles, triangles and trapeziums; trapezium area \(= \frac{1}{2}(a + b)h\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reading a velocity-time graph as a displacement-time graph: here a horizontal line means constant velocity, not "at rest".
2. Using slope for displacement or area for acceleration: slope gives acceleration, area gives displacement.
3. Adding \(A_{2}\) when displacement is asked (or subtracting it when distance is asked).
4. Taking the wrong height in a trapezium: the height is the distance between the two parallel sides (70 in BCDE of Example 6, not 0.5).
5. Mixing units, e.g. minutes with m/s.
